'''John Clive Ward''', {{post-nominals|size=100%|country=AUS|FRS}} (1 August 1924 – 6 May 2000) was an [[English Australians|Anglo-Australian]] [[physicist]] who made significant contributions to quantum field theory, condensed-matter physics, and statistical mechanics. [[Andrei Sakharov]] called Ward one of the titans of quantum electrodynamics.

Ward introduced the [[Ward–Takahashi identity]]. He was one of the authors of the [[Standard Model]] of gauge particle interactions: his contributions were published in a series of papers he co-authored with [[Abdus Salam]]. He is also credited with being an early advocate of the use of [[Feynman diagrams]]. It has been said that physicists have made use of his principles and developments "often without knowing it, and generally without quoting him."<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte" /> The [[Ising model]] was another one of his research interests.

In 1955, Ward was recruited to work at the [[Atomic Weapons Research Establishment]] at [[Aldermaston]]. There, he independently derived a version of the [[Teller–Ulam design]], for which he has been called the "father of the British H-bomb".<ref name=TIP />

==Early life==
John Clive Ward was born in [[East Ham]], [[London]],<ref name="memoirs">{{cite web |first=John Clive |last=Ward |title=Memoirs of a Theoretical Physicist |publisher=Optics Journal |location=Rochester, New York |year=2004 |url=http://www.laserreviewers.com/JCWard.pdf |access-date=2 January 2016}}</ref> on 1 August 1924.<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte" /> He was the son of Joseph William Ward, a [[civil servant]] who worked in [[Inland Revenue]],<ref name="memoirs" /><ref>{{London Gazette |date=2 May 1911 |issue=28490 |page=3340}}</ref> and his wife Winifred {{nee}} Palmer, a schoolteacher. He had a sister, Mary Patricia. He attended Chalkwell Elementary School and [[Westcliff High School for Boys]]. In 1938 he sat for and won a £100 scholarship to [[Bishop Stortford College]]. He  took the [[Higher School Certificate (England and Wales)|Higher School Certificate]] Examination in 1942, receiving distinctions in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry and Latin, and was offered a postmastership (scholarship) to [[Merton College, Oxford]].<ref name="memoirs" /><ref name="MCreg">{{cite book|editor1-last=Levens|editor1-first=R.G.C.|title=Merton College Register 1900–1964|date=1964|publisher=Basil Blackwell|location=Oxford|page=335}}</ref>

Although the [[Second World War]] was raging at the time, Ward was not called up by the Army, and was allowed to complete his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in Engineering Science with [[first class honours]], studying mathematics under [[J. H. C. Whitehead]] and [[E. C. Titchmarsh]]. He received a bursary from the Harmsworth Trust, and in October 1946, with the war over, secured a position as a graduate assistant to [[Maurice Pryce]], who had recently been appointed a professor of theoretical physics at Oxford.<ref name="memoirs" />

== Scientific contributions ==
Ward's total number of published papers was only about 20, a fact that reflects a strong sense of self-criticism. He was also critical of what he called "PhD factories" and expressed scepticism towards the importance attached to having a large number of citations.<ref name=AP2009 /> He never supervised graduate students.<ref name="memoirs"/> He received some significant awards, including the [[Faraday Medal and Prize|Guthrie Medal]] and [[Dirac Medal (UNSW)|Dirac Medal]] of the [[University of New South Wales]] in 1981, the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics|Heineman Prize]] in 1982, and the [[Hughes Medal]] in 1983 "for his highly influential and original contributions to quantum field theory, particularly the Ward identity and the Salam–Ward theory of weak interactions".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mq.edu.au/study/find-a-course/science/physics/john-clive-ward |title=John Clive Ward |publisher=[[Macquarie University]] |access-date=4 January 2017 |archive-date=4 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170104170255/http://www.mq.edu.au/study/find-a-course/science/physics/john-clive-ward |url-status=dead }}</ref> He became a [[fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1965.<ref name="memoirs"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dombey|first=Norman|date=2021|title=John Clive Ward. 1 August 1924—6 May 2000|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=70|pages=419–440 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2020.0023 |s2cid=231938446 |doi-access=free|arxiv=2007.16199}}</ref> 

[[Andrei Sakharov]] said Ward was one of the "titans" of quantum electrodynamics alongside [[Freeman Dyson]], [[Richard Feynman]], [[Julian Schwinger]], [[Sin-Itiro Tomonaga]] and [[Gian Carlo Wick]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Andrei |last=Sakharov |author-link=Andrei Sakharov |title=Memoirs |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |year=1990 |page=[https://archive.org/details/memoirs00sakh/page/84 84] |isbn=978-0-394-53740-5 |oclc=21303910 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/memoirs00sakh/page/84 }}</ref> In this regard, it has been said that physicists have made use of his principles and developments "often without knowing it, and generally without quoting him."<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte" />

===Quantum entanglement===
In 1947, Ward and Pryce published a paper in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'',  in which they were the first to calculate, and use, [[probability amplitude]]s for the polarisation of a pair of [[Quantum entanglement|quantum entangled]] [[photon]]s moving in opposite directions.<ref name=W1947>{{cite journal |first1=M. H. L. |last1=Pryce |first2=J. C. |last2=Ward |title=Angular Correlation Effects with Annihilation Radiation |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=160 |issue=4065 |page=435 |year=1947 |doi=10.1038/160435a0 |bibcode=1947Natur.160..435P |s2cid=4101513 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=D2012>{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |author-link=F. J. Duarte |title=The Origin of Quantum Entanglement Experiments Based on Polarization Measurements |journal=The European Physical Journal H |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=311–318 |year=2012 |doi=10.1140/epjh/e2012-20047-y|bibcode=2012EPJH...37..311D |s2cid=122007033 }}</ref> For polarisations ''x'' and ''y'', Ward derived this probability amplitude to be:<ref name=D2012/>
:<math>\left|\psi\right\rang=(\left|x,y\right\rang - \left|y,x\right\rang ) </math>
which can be [[Normalization (statistics)|normalised]] as:<ref name=D2012/><ref name=QOE>{{cite book |title= Quantum Optics for Engineers | publisher= CRC |location=New York |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-4398-8853-7 |oclc=871400712 | first = F. J. |last= Duarte |author-link=F. J. Duarte |page=273 }}</ref>
:<math>\left|\psi\right\rang= {1 \over \sqrt{2}}(\left|x\right\rang_{1} \left|y\right\rang_{2}- \left|y\right\rang_{1} \left|x\right\rang_{2}) </math>
This can be used to derive the correlation of polarisation of the two photons.<ref name=W1947/> Their prediction was confirmed experimentally by [[Chien-Shiung Wu]] and I. Shaknov in 1950.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Wu |first1=C. S.
 |last2=Shaknov |first2=I.
 |year=1950
 |title=The Angular Correlation of Scattered Annihilation Radiation
 |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_physical-review_1950-01-01_77_1/page/136 |journal=[[Physical Review]]
 |volume=77 |issue=1
 |pages=136
 |bibcode=1950PhRv...77..136W
 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.77.136
}}</ref> This was the first experimental confirmation of a pair of entangled photons as applicable to the [[EPR paradox|Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen (EPR) paradox]].<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Dalitz |first1=R. H.
 |author1-link=Richard Dalitz
 |last2=Duarte |first2=F. J.
 |year=2000
 |title=John Clive Ward
 |journal=[[Physics Today]]
 |volume=53 |issue=10 |pages=99
 |bibcode=2000PhT....53j..99D
 |doi=10.1063/1.1325207
 |doi-access=free
}}</ref> The result was subsequently explained by [[Richard Dalitz]] and [[F. J. Duarte|Frank Duarte]].<ref name=D2012/><ref name="Dalitz and Duarte" /><ref>{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |author-link=F. J. Duarte |title=The Probability Amplitude for Entangled Polarizations: an Interferometric Approach |journal=Journal of Modern Optics |volume=60 |issue=8 |pages=1585–1587 |year=2013 |doi=10.1080/09500340.2013.844282|bibcode=2013JMOp...60.1585D |s2cid=121059369 }}</ref> Apparently following [[Paul Dirac|Dirac's]] doctrine, Ward was never bothered by issues of [[Interpretations of quantum mechanics|interpretation in quantum mechanics]].<ref name=QOE />

With his Harmsworth scholarship expiring, and seeing few prospects at Oxford, Ward responded to a job advertisement from the [[University of Sydney]]. He was offered a position, but when he arrived, found that it was for a tutor, and not a [[lecturer]]. He therefore served out the year, then returned to Oxford to complete his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (D.Phil.) thesis on "Some Properties of the Elementary Particles". Ward expected that his thesis, an elaboration of his 1947 paper, would be easily approved by the external examiner, [[Nicholas Kemmer]], but at the last minute Kemmer's place was taken by [[Rudolf Peierls]], who refused to accept it. Only after a forceful argument by the internal examiner, J. de Witt, was the thesis awarded.<ref name="memoirs"/><ref name="JCW1949">{{cite thesis|first=J. C.|last=Ward|title=Some Properties of Elementary Particles|degree=D. Phil.|publisher=Oxford University|year=1949|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/OXVU1:LSCOP_OX:oxfaleph020288298|access-date=2 January 2017}}</ref>

===Ward identity===
Pryce arranged for Ward to receive an award from the [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (United Kingdom)|Department of Scientific and Industrial Research]] (DSIR) for two years. It was then that he developed the [[Ward–Takahashi identity]], originally known as "Ward Identity" (or "Ward's Identities").<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte">{{cite journal|last1=Dalitz |first1=Richard H. |author-link=Richard Dalitz |last2=Duarte |first2=Frank J. |author-link2=F. J. Duarte |title=John Clive Ward|journal=Physics Today|date=October 2000|volume=53|issue=10|pages=99–100|doi=10.1063/1.1325207|bibcode = 2000PhT....53j..99D |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="memoirs"/><ref>{{cite journal|author=J. C. Ward|title=An identity in quantum electrodynamics|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=78|issue=2|pages=182|year=1950|url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.78.182|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.78.182|bibcode = 1950PhRv...78..182W |url-access=subscription}}</ref> This result in [[quantum electrodynamics]] was inspired by a conjecture of [[Freeman Dyson]],<ref>{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Dyson |author-link=Freeman Dyson |title=The S matrix in Quantum Electrodynamics |journal=Physical Review |volume=75 |issue=21 |pages=1736–1755 |year=1949 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.75.1736 |bibcode=1949PhRv...75.1736D }}</ref> and was disclosed in a one-half-page letter typical of Ward's succinct style.  In their book ''Quantum Electrodynamics'', [[Walter Greiner]] and {{interlanguage link|Joachim Reinhardt|de}} state in their discussion of charge [[renormalisation]]: "the Ward Identity has a much more fundamental significance: it ensures the ''universality of the electromagnetic interaction''."<ref>{{cite book |first1=Walter |last1=Greiner |author-link=Walter Greiner |first2=Joachim |last2=Reinhardt |title=Quantum Electrodynamics |url=https://archive.org/details/quantumelectrody00grei_605 |url-access=limited |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin |year=2009 |isbn=978-3-540-87560-4 |oclc=920255774 |page=[https://archive.org/details/quantumelectrody00grei_605/page/n332 319]}}</ref> In his book ''The Infinity Puzzle'', [[Frank Close]] wrote: "Ward's Identities are the basic foundations on which the entire edifice of renormalisation rests."<ref name=TIP>{{cite book |first=Frank |last=Close |author-link=Frank Close |title=The Infinity Puzzle |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |year=2011 |page=90 |isbn=978-0-19-959350-7 }}</ref>

In 1950, Ward's DSIR fellowship was coming to an end. Pryce had become a visiting professor at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], and Ward's colleagues [[P. T. Matthews]] and [[Abdus Salam]] were visiting members there in the 1950–1951 academic year. Through them, he was able to secure a $3,000 membership for the 1951–1952 academic year. It was at Princeton that he was introduced to the [[Ising Model]], and met [[Mark Kac]] from [[Cornell University]], with whom he would collaborate on an exact solution of the Ising model using a combinatorial method.<ref name="memoirs"/><ref name=KW1952>{{cite journal |author-link=Mark Kac|first1=M. |last1=Kac |first2=J. C. |last2=Ward |title=A Combinatorial Solution of the Two-Dimensional Ising Model |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_physical-review_1952-12-15_88_6/page/1332|journal=Physical Review |volume=88 |issue=6 |pages=1332–1337 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.88.1332 |year=1952|bibcode=1952PhRv...88.1332K }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=R. B. |last1=Potts |first2=J. C. |last2=Ward |title=The Combinatorial Method and the Two-Dimensional Ising Model |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |volume=13 |issue=1 Year=1955 |pages=38–46 |year=1955 |doi=10.1143/PTP.13.38 |bibcode=1955PThPh..13...38P |doi-access=free }}</ref> His joint work with Kac on the Ising Model gave rise to what is now being called the Kac-Ward operator.<ref name=KW1952 /><ref>{{cite journal |first=L. O. |last=Chekhov |title=A Spectral Problem on Graphs and L-Functions |journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys |volume=54 |issue=6 |pages=1197–1232 |year=1999 |doi=10.1070/RM1999v054n06ABEH000231|arxiv=cond-mat/9911244 |bibcode=1999RuMaS..54.1197C |s2cid=18689477 }}</ref> When his membership ended he worked for the [[Bell Laboratories]] in 1952 and 1953.<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte" /> He then accepted an offer of a lectureship at the [[University of Adelaide]] from [[Herbert S. Green|Bert Green]], where he worked for a year before taking up another membership at the Institute for Advanced Study.<ref name="memoirs"/>

===Standard Model===
[[Image:Fermi Surface.svg|thumb|right|[[Luttinger's theorem]] (introduced by [[J. M. Luttinger]] and Ward) relates a [[Fermi liquid theory|Fermi liquid]]'s particle density to the volume enclosed by its Fermi surface.]]
Ward left the British hydrogen bomb programme and took a job with an electronics company in California. Later in 1956, [[Elliott Montroll]] offered him a visiting professorship at the [[University of Maryland]].<ref name="memoirs" /> Noting a recent paper by [[Keith Brueckner]] and [[Murray Gell-Mann]] on the ground state energy of an [[Fermi gas|electron gas]], Ward gave a lecture in which he proposed a different approach. Montroll recognised that this was [[Debye–Hückel theory]]. Over the next few weeks, Ward later recalled, "We had managed not only to produce a definitive extension of a previously purely classical theory, but also to establish the rules for diagrammatic treatment of problems in quantum statistical mechanics, rules that are now the bread and butter of modern calculations."<ref name="memoirs" />

Soon after, physicists were rocked by the news that Wu and [[Tsung-Dao Lee]] had demonstrated in the [[Wu experiment]] that [[Parity (physics)#Parity violation|parity is not conserved]] in [[weak interactions]]. This inspired Ward to consider particle physics again. Along with many others, he consider how [[gauge theory]] could be applied to [[Fermi's theory of beta decay]].<ref name="memoirs" /> Ward became one of the authors of the [[Standard Model]] of gauge particle interactions; his contributions on electromagnetic and weak interactions were published in a series of papers he co-authored with [[Abdus Salam]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Salam|first1=A.|author-link=Abdus Salam|last2=Ward|first2=J. C.|year=1959|title=Weak and electromagnetic interactions|journal=Nuovo Cimento|volume=11|issue=4|pages=568–577|bibcode=1959NCim...11..568S|doi=10.1007/BF02726525}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Salam|first1=A.|author-link=Abdus Salam|last2=Ward|first2=J. C.|year=1961|title=On a gauge theory of elementary interactions|journal=Nuovo Cimento|volume=19|issue=1|pages=165–170|bibcode=1961NCim...19..165S|doi=10.1007/BF02812723|s2cid=122962512}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Salam|first1=A.|author-link=Abdus Salam|last2=Ward|first2=J. C.|year=1964|title=Electromagnetic and weak interactions|journal=Physics Letters|volume=13|issue=2|pages=168–171|bibcode=1964PhL....13..168S|doi=10.1016/0031-9163(64)90711-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Salam|first1=A.|author-link=Abdus Salam|last2=Ward|first2=J. C.|year=1964|title=Gauge theory of elementary interactions|journal=Physical Review|volume=136|issue=3B|pages=B763–B768|bibcode=1964PhRv..136..763S|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.136.B763}}</ref> Ward wrote a note to Abdus, informing him that [[Albert Einstein]] would be [[Spin (physics)|spinning]] in his grave, presumably clockwise.<ref name="memoirs" />

The contributions of Salam and Ward to the Standard Model were used in the development of the theoretical structure of the [[Higgs boson]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Higgs|first=P. W.|author-link=Peter Higgs|year=1966|title=Spontaneous Symmetry Breakdown Without Massless Bosons|journal=Physical Review|volume=145|issue=4|pages=1156–1163|bibcode=1966PhRv..145.1156H|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.145.1156|doi-access=free}}</ref> Ward also made contributions to [[quantum mechanics]],<ref name="JCW1949" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Montroll|first1=E. W.|author-link=Elliott Waters Montroll|last2=Ward|first2=J. C.|year=1958|title=Quantum Statistics of Interacting Particles; General Theory and Some Remarks on Properties of an Electron Gas|journal=The Physics of Fluids|volume=1|issue=1|bibcode=1958PhFl....1...55M|doi=10.1063/1.1724337|pages=55–72}}</ref> fermion theory,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Luttinger|first1=J. M.|author-link=Joaquin Mazdak Luttinger|last2=Ward|first2=J. C.|year=1960|title=Ground-State Energy and Many-Fermion System|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_physical-review_1960-06-01_118_5/page/1416|journal=Physical Review|volume=118|issue=5|pages=1417–1427|bibcode=1960PhRv..118.1417L|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.118.1417}}</ref> quantum [[solid-state physics]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ward|first1=J. C.|last2=Wilks|first2=J.|year=1952|title=Second Sound and the Thermo-Mechanical Effect at Very Low Temperatures|journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science|volume=43|issue=336|pages=48–50|doi=10.1080/14786440108520965}}</ref> and [[statistical mechanics]] and the Ising model.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Montroll|first1=E. W.|last2=Potts|first2=R. B.|last3=Ward|first3=J. C.|year=1963|title=Correlations and Spontaneous Magnetization of the Two-Dimensional Ising Model|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics|volume=4|issue=2|pages=308–322|bibcode=1963JMP.....4..308M|doi=10.1063/1.1703955}}</ref>

==Aldermaston==
In 1955, Ward was recruited by [[William Cook (scientist)|William Cook]] to work on the [[British hydrogen bomb programme]] at the [[Atomic Weapons Research Establishment]] at [[Aldermaston]]. The British government had decided that it needed [[hydrogen bomb]]s, and it was Aldermaston's task to design one.<ref name="Britain and the H-Bomb" /> Cook had been put in charge of the project in September 1954. Ward was the only theoretical physicist at Aldermaston; the director, [[William Penney]], although a physicist, was an expert on [[hydrodynamics]] and instrumentation.  Penney was not happy to have Ward forced on him, and the two did not get along.<ref name="Bluff">{{cite journal |journal=London Review of Books |date=22 October 1992 |title=Britain's Thermonuclear Bluff |first1=Norman |last1=Dombey |first2=Eric |last2=Grove |url=http://www.reformation.org/british-thermonuclear-bluff.html |access-date=4 January 2017 }}</ref> [[John Corner]] recalled that Ward did not fit in at Aldermaston.<ref name="Britain and the H-Bomb" />

British knowledge of thermonuclear designs was limited to the work done by the wartime  [[Manhattan Project]]: [[Edward Teller]]'s [[History of the Teller–Ulam design|Classic Super]],<ref name="memoirs"/> and a 1946 design by [[John von Neumann]] and [[Klaus Fuchs]]. All that was known for certain about the American hydrogen bomb design was that it had multiple stages.<ref name="Britain and the H-Bomb" /> "I was assigned", Ward later recalled, "the improbable job of uncovering the secret of the Ulam–Teller invention&nbsp;... an idea of genius far beyond the talents of the personnel at Aldermaston, a fact well-known to both Cook and Penney."<ref name="Bluff"/>

After working through a large number of proposals, Ward hit upon a workable design incorporating staging, compression and radiation implosion.<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte" /><ref name="Bluff"/> At a meeting on 2 December 1955, Ward sketched it on the blackboard. Penny's response was cool, regarding it as too complicated, but Cook recognised it as worthy. Although Ward's design was not the one ultimately adopted for the hydrogen bombs used in [[Operation Grapple]], the concept was influential,<ref name="memoirs"/><ref name="Britain and the H-Bomb">{{cite book |first1=Lorna |last1=Arnold |author-link=Lorna Arnold |first2=Katherine |last2=Pyne |author-link2=Kate Pyne |title=Britain and the H-Bomb |publisher=Palgrave |location=Basingstoke |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-333-73685-2 |oclc=925315618 |pages=80–88, 244–245 }}</ref> and the development of a more advanced design than the Americans had would be the key to achieving the overall objective of the project—a resumption of the nuclear [[Special Relationship]] with the Americans.<ref name="Bluff"/><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/a-myth-exploded-we-did-not-bluff-to-gain-the-bomb-britain-did-have-the-worlds-ultimate-weapon-within-1448335.html |access-date=3 January 2017 |date=12 September 1994 |newspaper=The Independent |title=A myth exploded: we did not bluff to gain the Bomb: Britain did have the world's ultimate weapon within its grasp in the Fifties, says Brian Cathcart |first=Brian |last=Cathcart |author-link=Brian Cathcart }}</ref> He has been called the "father of the British H-bomb".<ref name=TIP />

==Macquarie University==
After Maryland, Ward looked for a new job. He thought he had found one at the [[University of Miami]] in [[Florida]], but was denied tenure and left in 1959. He then secured a position at [[Carnegie Mellon University]] in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]], but was unhappy there. He applied once again for a one-year membership at the Institute for Advanced Study, and was accepted for a third time. [[Theodore H. Berlin]] then offered him a position at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1961. He remained until 1966, when he answered an advertisement for a mathematics professor at [[Victoria University of Wellington]] in New Zealand. Australian friends were astounded that anyone would choose New Zealand over Australia. At [[Macquarie University]] in [[Sydney]] he was welcomed by Professor [[Peter Mason (physicist)|Peter Mason]] in 1968 with a professorial appointment. He turned down offers from Oxford and Cambridge.<ref name="memoirs"/><ref name="Dalitz and Duarte"/> He eventually became an Australian citizen.<ref name=AP2009 />

In 1967 he created the physics program at Macquarie University using the [[Feynman Lectures on Physics]] as primary textbooks.  This program had a strong experimental emphasis and Ward himself (who originally was trained as an engineer) "had great admiration for anything practical".<ref name=AP2009>{{cite journal |url=http://www.tunablelasers.com/AUSTRALIAN%20PHYSICS%2046%286%29%20171-175%20%282009%29.pdf |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |author-link=F. J. Duarte |title=The man behind an identity in quantum electrodynamics |journal=Australian Physics |volume=46 |issue=6 |pages=171–175 |year=2009}}</ref> He is credited with being an early pioneer in the use of [[Feynman diagrams]], and spreading their use in Australia.<ref>{{cite book |first=David |last=Kaiser |author-link=David Kaiser (physicist) |title=Drawing Theories Apart: The Dispersion of Feynman Diagrams in Postwar Physics |url=https://archive.org/details/drawingtheoriesa00kais |url-access=limited |pages=[https://archive.org/details/drawingtheoriesa00kais/page/n141 121]–124 |publisher=University of Chicago |location=Chicago |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-226-42266-4}}</ref> In the late 1970s Ward participated, with Frank Duarte, in the successful [[Macquarie science reform movement]],<ref>{{cite book |first1=B. |last1=Mansfield |first2=M. |last2=Hutchinson |title=Liberality of Opportunity: A History of Macquarie University 1964–1989 |publisher=Hale and Iremonger |location=Sydney |year=1992 |pages=115–118 }}</ref> and considered this a "most important accomplishment".<ref name=AP2009/>  The most visible sign was that the university agreed to present [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) degrees instead of just Bachelor of Arts (BA) degrees, the former being more highly prized by students and workplaces in Australia.<ref name="memoirs"/>

==Personal life and death==
Besides his physics, Ward played the piano and the [[French horn]].  Ward played the piano at public performances, for example, in  August 1968 playing Grieg at Blacktown Town Hall, Sydney. He was a bachelor for most of his life, but he was briefly married while in the US. He had no children.<ref name="memoirs"/> He died on [[Vancouver Island]] in [[British Columbia]], Canada, on 6 May 2000, from a respiratory illness.<ref name="Dalitz and Duarte"/>
